speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: It will be known as SkillsFuture Singapore, or SSG in short, a new abbreviation to remember.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: This is a journey which started decades ago, which I would broadly categorise into three phases.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: From the first phase, broadly from the 1950s to the 1970s, we were learning to survive.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: The key imperatives were to impart basic employability skills, raise levels of literacy and numeracy, and stem high unemployment rates.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: The Adult Education Board, or better known as Lembaga to many Singaporeans, was formed in 1960 to train our adult workforce.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Singapore Polytechnic and Ngee Ann Polytechnic were also established during this period.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: In the 1980s, we were moving up the value chain, contending for choice investments and learning to compete.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Many key elements of the supporting infrastructure for lifelong learning were born during this period.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: For example, the Skills Development Fund (SDF) was established in 1979 to support workforce skills upgrading.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: The Vocational and Industrial Training Board (VITB), which evolved into the present-day Institute of Technical Education (ITE), was also founded then in 1979.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: The German, French and Japan-Singapore Institutes, set up with the help of multinational corporations (MNCs), were combined to form Nanyang Polytechnic.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: By the turn of the century, Singapore's economy had already achieved significant breadth as well as depth.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: So, we entered the third phase, which is learning for life.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: The public education and training landscape evolved into one of many pathways that an individual may choose to pursue.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: We established more institutions, such as the Republic Polytechnic and the Singapore Institute of Technology (SIT).

speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Existing institutions started to roll out various programmes, part-time, full-time, pre- and post-employment training, across many industry sectors and career stages.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: At the same time, the Government established the Singapore Workforce Development Agency (WDA) in 2003 and helped to accelerate a shift from an employer-centric skills adult training system, to one that placed greater focus on the individual.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: WDA worked with private training providers to set up Continuing Education and Training Centres, or CET Centres, which offered subsidised training directly to workers.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Such supply-side interventions meant that training subsidies were made directly available to individuals, with or without their employers' sponsorship.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: The learning for life phase is therefore most notable for empowering individuals, and encouraging each one of us to pursue our interests and what we are best at.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: First, we have developed a high-quality education and training landscape, anchored by strong institutions, both in the public and private domain.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Second, we have started to draw tighter linkages between work and training, by encouraging the participation of employers in 	Page: 47 skills development and ensuring the relevance of skills training programmes.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Third, we have also started the shift towards greater individual ownership and empowerment.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: This is not for administrative or bureaucratic neatness but is to draw better synergies between the work of MOE and SSG.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Under SkillsFuture, these institutions will expand their range of programmes to support skills deepening for adult learners, by offering more bite-sized and industry-relevant courses.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: These can be delivered through centres or units within those institutions dedicated to adult training and lifelong learning.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: As a Statutory Board under MOE, SSG will coordinate and increase the range and quality of these skills-based training programmes offered by both the Post-Secondary Education Institutions (PSEIs) and private training providers.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: The second priority is to integrate work and study for a responsive skills training ecosystem.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: This is something that is already in progress.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: For instance, WDA currently champions the SkillsFuture Earn-and-Learn Programme, in which fresh polytechnic and ITE graduates undergo on-the-job and classroom training to deepen their skills.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Today, MOE is expanding and enhancing its education and career counselling services in schools and Institutes of Higher Learning (IHLs).

speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: WDA has, over the years, built up capacity to advise workers on career options, training pathways and assist them in their job search.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: This is an area that requires more work as there is a greater interest amongst adult workers now to go for training because of SkillsFuture Credit.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Under this new structure, all these resources from WDA today will be grouped under SSG.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: So, the third priority is that as work and study grow to form more of a seamless continuum, there can be greater coordination between SSG and the education and career counsellors in education institutions to help all learners, students as well as workers, to discover their strengths 	Page: 48 and interests, chart their learning pathways and their careers.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: The fourth priority is to expand skills-based progression pathways by facilitating the interoperability of qualifications.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: As far as possible, what you learn under one qualification system can be recognised by other qualification systems.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: This will better ensure that every training achievement is a step forward, in a system where there are no dead ends.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: In the coming months and years, SSG will drive the advancement of such arrangements and bring about interoperability of qualifications across the education and training landscape, at a systemic level.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Today, WDA and CPE are separate Statutory Boards that run different quality assurance and regulatory frameworks for adult training and private education sectors respectively.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: The considerations for regulating adult training and private education are somewhat different, but we can rationalise and streamline wherever we can to reduce duplication and for better efficiency.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: These changes can take effect by the time SSG is formed.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Part Two establishes the SSG Agency and details the powers and functions of SSG.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Clause 5 under Part Two outlines the functions of SSG.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: In the performance of its functions, SSG will address the current, emerging and future workforce skills requirements, ensure a responsive system of education and training, and look into increasing workforce productivity and Singapore's international competitiveness.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: I will now describe in detail some of the key functions of SSG.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: First, SSG will facilitate skills acquisition and lifelong learning through planning and developing policies, programmes and services that provide or support the provision of adult and further education; promoting a national approach to such education and general enthusiasm for lifelong learning; undertaking research relating to such education; and identifying the key skills and competencies needed by the Singapore workforce.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Second, SSG will facilitate the improvement of quality of courses in adult education or further education provided in Singapore.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: This can include accrediting or facilitating accreditation of providers of adult or further education.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Third, SSG will foster and ensure the collaboration between SSG and WSG where there are areas of synergies.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: This SSG function will be enabled by a specific clause in the Bill on cooperation and collaboration with WSG.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: The same clause is also mirrored in the Singapore Workforce Development Agency (Amendment) Bill that has been passed.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Clause 6 describes the powers accorded to SSG to allow it to carry out the stated functions which I have just described.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Other general powers of Statutory Boards, such as the power to enter 	Page: 49 into agreements and enact financial decisions and so on, are also included.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: I will now deal with Part Three to Six of the Bill, which set out the corporate structure and governance of SSG, and the personnel and financial provisions.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Part Three provides for the appointment of the Chairperson, Deputy Chairperson and other members of the governance board of SSG, their tenure, remuneration, conditions for qualification, as well as conflict of interest disclosure requirements.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Part Four sets out the procedures for meetings of the governing board.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Clauses 34 to 36 under this Part provide for the appointment of committees for purposes which are better regulated and managed by committees.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: SSG can delegate the performance or exercise of any of its functions or powers to such committees, amongst others.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Part Five covers personnel matters, including the appointment of the Chief Executive, the treatment of employees as public servants for the purposes of the Penal Code, the need for preservation of secrecy, and the protection from personal liability for performing, in good faith and with reasonable care, functions under this Bill.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Part Six of the Bill provides for financial provisions of SSG and contains the standard provisions found in the Acts of other Statutory Boards.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Part Seven deals with the administration and enforcement powers of SSG.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: The powers are largely similar to those provided for the performance of functions under WDA today.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: With the establishment of SSG, there could be overlaps between the stated functions of SSG and ITE today, as well as between SSG and the Standards, Productivity and Innovation Board (SPRING).

speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: This will ensure a responsive and industry-relevant system of education and training, in which every person is a lifelong learner in the pursuit of skills mastery.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: As I studied this Bill, which I understand is meant to be operational in nature, I cannot help but feel that there is nothing very exciting mentioned on either skills or the future.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: It belies the significance of SkillsFuture as a national movement to provide Singaporeans with the opportunities to develop their fullest potential throughout life, regardless of their starting point.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: The SkillsFuture website promises that a variety of resources will be deployed to help Singaporeans own a better future with skills mastery and lifelong learning.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: I, therefore, hope that when the Bill is passed, the tone of the Act is merely an understatement of the exciting mission and breakthroughs that SSG is expected to deliver.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Kudos to the many supporters of the SkillsFuture team and the many agencies behind it.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: So much has indeed happened since the SkillsFuture movement was launched two years ago.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: While all the pieces make sense each time they are presented, I fear the day when we cannot see the forest for the trees.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: As a member of the former SkillsFuture Council and now the combined Council for Skills, Innovation and Productivity (CSIP), I have sat through enough meetings led by the Chairman Deputy Prime Minister Tharman Shamugaratnam, to "double confirm" that the intent of the SkillsFuture movement is to future-proof the skills of Singaporeans and Singapore businesses.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: The Minister himself, no less, said that people often mistake SkillsFuture for a funding scheme, training programme or an organisation.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: He said it is not any of those.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Rather, it is "everything we do to create a future that is different and better than today, in the way we look at work and careers, and the way we develop ourselves and our next generation".

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: SkillsFuture is not simply about tapping on the $500 Credit to attend the big menu of courses at our Community Centres.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: As they say, "Don't use, so wasted!" or in Mandarin,"不用白不用".

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: It is not simply an active ageing programme.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: It is not just a scheme to persuade one to either not sign up for university or to sign up later.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: It is not about reviving the Training, Consulting or Mentoring industries.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: It is not just about doing up Sectoral Human Resource Manpower Plans to see how we can attract more talents for each selected industry sector.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: It is not just about doing the same thing that we have to do anyway and then branding it as SkillsFuture – what I would term "old wine in new wine skin".

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: SkillsFuture has to be more than all that I have mentioned.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: And the new SSG Agency established with the passing of this Bill, must live up to its name – focus on Skills and Future!

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: All members of the agency must envision the future of the industry, of our nation and future-proof the skills of our Singaporeans.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: As it scrutinises the current and potential initiatives, SSG must administer the acid test of whether all these ideas will help Singaporeans future-proof themselves and maximise their 	Page: 51 potential.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: We must strive towards the day when fewer and fewer of our people and businesses are surprised when they find that their jobs or those of their loved ones become irrelevant or, worse, suddenly disappear, disrupted by business models or technologies or the sharing economy revolution that we did not see coming; or did not do anything about even if we knew they were coming.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: The new SSG agency is, therefore, our bastion of hope to secure our future; to ensure that the major remains the major and not lose focus that we are trying to build a future for our people.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: First, on building strong expertise in the three critical pillars of Content, Pedagogy and Assessment.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: We need to abandon the traditional mindset of discarding or hijacking ideas that are "not invented here".

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: There is no way that career educators, who are used to working within the confines of school buildings, systems or classrooms, can hold the monopoly of ideas.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Next, on SSG's expertise on Pedagogy or How to Deliver Learning.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: I spoke on how our students, many of whom are digital natives, cannot be left to learn only as far as their adult teachers can or will learn.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: I spoke on how best education resources and best practices must be made available online and otherwise so that more learners can access them, to level the playing field.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: I spoke about the potential of an open architecture to which content developers can contribute, where content can be curated and transformed into modules that can be distributed to more learners.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: I am not the only one thinking about this.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: At the tertiary level, I have observed different IHLs trying out different Learning Management Systems, some of them re-inventing the wheels of locating, negotiating the best platforms.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: I believe it is the role of the Government and, in this case, the SSG agency, to consolidate and share these learnings in pedagogy as I fear that by the time we think we are ready, the game is over and our investments hitherto would have been wasted.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Building SSG's expertise on Assessment or How to Test if One Has Learnt or Mastered a Skill.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: But because PSEIs are a close link to the industry, how we assess and report on results will become the proxy by which employers evaluate the candidates they seek to employ.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Next, for the Minister's consideration, to become the Uber for certain service gaps in the post-Secondary education space, such as in special education.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: At this point, Madam, I want to remind the Ministry about the scope of this Bill, on whom this Bill is meant for.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: It is not a Bill just to future-proof those who can study in the existing PSEIs.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: We do not leave behind those who are at risk.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: We do not throw the crumbs while the rest of us feast and continue to learn what others do not.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Every one of us deserves to maximise our potential, whatever level that potential is deemed to be.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Our Singapore brand of lifelong learning must be inclusive.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: The cliff-effect of learners, especially those who graduate from special schools, is real.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: The cost of not helping them to continue learning and to renew their skills is high as they may otherwise seek higher cost social services, such as day activity centres, because they are no more relevant to the workforce.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: There is also an upside in that a number of adults with special needs may be able to take on jobs in our very tight labour market.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: But even those with special needs who found jobs earlier, will find that without continual customised training and support, they will soon lose their jobs.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: The current efforts by SG Enable need more boosting and scale.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: SkillsFuture for this group of Singaporeans is necessary but may have to innovatively take on a different complexion, with strong collaboration between SSG and other relevant Government agencies, voluntary welfare organisations and the private sector.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: This Academy, which may be a blend of physical and online presence, need not provide content itself, just like what Uber does, it does not own any vehicle.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: It should work with the key disability groups for proper needs analysis and development of curriculum and learning solutions for persons with special learning needs.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: It must align with the Bill's intent to focus on skills and the future.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: And, lastly, for the Minister's consideration, to be Bold to Create and Chase Our Own Rainbow.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: We have spoken for too long about our admiration for the German and Swiss vocational and training systems.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: These systems are backed by a culture of centuries of ingrained mindsets that honour craftsmen and strong private-public education ventures.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: They are not hindered by bias that has plagued us for generations: our bias against sometimes blue-collar workers and our love for scholars and white-collar jobs.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Let us forget about trying to become like the Germans and the Swiss.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: I suspect that in the future, the dichotomy between vocational, applied education and academic pathways will be blurred.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: So, let us gather a group of dream-makers and chase the rainbow, and create our very own Singapore excellence model in post-secondary education.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: A dream that will allow us to master skills to not just make excellent products and services like the Germans and Swiss, but also to market them well like the Americans, in the case 	Page: 53 of Uber, Airbnb and so forth.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: I am confident that SSG, under the Minister's guidance and the team behind him, can blaze the trail for post-secondary education, but only if it will not simply do business as usual.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: I am prepared to be part of the solution to contribute to SSG's purpose to secure the future of Singaporeans.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: And I guess Singapore can count on us.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Clearly, in the 21st Century, these are all critical arenas for us to succeed in as a people and as an economy.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We do need to take adult education and training far more seriously to enhance economic goals and also individual career progression.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: It makes sense from the standpoint of our economy, as well as from the standpoint of individual self-actualisation.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I believe others have commented on this point frequently.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In this way, Mdm Speaker, we can really enhance the effectiveness and national return on investment of SkillsFuture year by year, as opposed to merely highlighting good outcomes that may or may not be directly tied to the actual programmes.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I do have a suggestion in this regard.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: There is a large base of local education and training providers and this represents an economic opportunity as well.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: With the support of SSG, we could create training content that not only enhances employment outcomes for Singaporeans, but will also become exportable services that help drive economic 	Page: 54 growth and good job creation at home.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: There is also an industry that undertakes high-quality translation of such content in the Asian languages like Chinese and Malay.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The new SSG could work with economic agencies to grow this translation industry in Singapore to generate foreign source income streams.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Lastly, I would like to highlight one particular group of stakeholders that would benefit from SSG, which is Singaporeans who are serving their prison terms within our penal system.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: And if such Singaporeans could benefit from such training while they are serving their terms, that would make it better for their prospects, rehabilitation and help them to integrate better into the economy as productive contributors to the economy, perhaps even as entrepreneurs upon their release.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I would urge SSG to consider this particular group and to take that on as one particular goal that it addresses.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: The SkillsFuture movement seeks to prepare Singaporeans for a future that places new demands on jobs and earning a livelihood.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: The institutionalisation of SkillsFuture shows that it is not just another policy to be implemented, but it is a movement critical in charting our future.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: For this movement to be pervasive and sustainable, it must have, at its core, a mission to provide better jobs and better lives for Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: There is much to be said about learning and acquiring skills and knowledge as an end in itself.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: In fact, this intrinsic thirst for learning is critical to mastery and job security.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: But for the movement to build momentum and gain traction, it must, first, be able to translate how training and learning can lead to better jobs and better job security especially in this current economic climate.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: In the Labour Movement, during our interactions with workers, the most asked questions are: how can these courses help me to get better wages?

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: How can learning this help me to find the next job?

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: And are these the future skills that we need to stay secure?

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Answering these questions allow people to see how SkillsFuture can positively change their lives.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: With MOE overseeing SkillsFuture, how can we ensure that this will not only be a movement for the younger Singaporeans?

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: There is a need to prepare our young Singaporeans for jobs that do not exist today.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: But we should also focus on our current workforce.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: How will the new agency work with WSG, MOM, employers and unions so that the agency can be in touch with the type of skills that are needed in the workforce now and tomorrow?

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Indeed, perhaps, it is the work with the existing workforce that will result in substantive productivity gains 	Page: 55 that Singapore is striving for.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: This is a good initiative but understandably limited in scope and capacity as it is still new.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: How would initiatives, such as ELP, scaled up to reach a bigger group of graduates nationally?

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: Although SkillsFuture is in many ways unique, Singapore has not been alone in awakening to the urgent need to plug the skills gap in the labour market.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: Many countries, especially advanced economies, are concerned about the gap between workforce skills levels and those demanded by employers.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: In South Korea, for instance, the government has given industry a leading role in creating a set of National Competency Standards for job competencies, which the state then certifies and disseminates.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: In September 2013, South Korea also introduced its "Work-Study Dual System" of 	Page: 56 apprenticeship training.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: And just recently, in July, the then-Skills Minister of the United Kingdom (UK) announced a radical overhaul of their system of technical education.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: Thousands of courses which are considered ineffective are now being replaced, with the system simplified to provide 15 high-quality routes.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: More importantly, employers will be setting the standards.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: In the future landscape which these countries and we are trying to prepare for, growth rates will have to be eked out despite slowing population growth, an ageing workforce and disruptive technological advances.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: The challenges are already apparent in many ways, such as with polarisation in the jobs market, leading to a hollowing out at the mid-skills level.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: The structure of employment opportunities is changing to produce significantly different rates of job creation at different points of the skills spectrum.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: At one extreme, employment and earnings prospects for the highly trained PMET roles have been surging ahead for quite a while.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: At the other extreme, there has been a high demand for low-skilled manpower for many years and this was, to some extent, met by foreign manpower infusions.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: In fact, I strongly believe this was one of the main factors which influenced our reliance on foreign manpower for many years.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: This is similar to the observation in advanced economies like the United States (US) of improved jobs opportunities at both the high and low ends of the skills spectrum, but a significant deterioration in opportunities for middle-skill jobs.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: Even in China, which is the last country we would expect to worry about labour shortages, we see the manufacturing sector there turning to robotisation, a fact which the Minister for Finance recently explained in this House during his Budget round-up speech.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: Although China is not yet an advanced economy, its economy has been developing so rapidly that certain sectors, such as those in high-end manufacturing, are displaying signs of the same polarisation phenomenon I have mentioned earlier.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: When we look more closely at Singapore, Madam, we find that at the top end, the demand for highly-skilled workers is not being fully met by the supply from our tertiary-trained cohorts, mainly because our small population cannot cater to every niche area of specialisation.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: At the low end of the skills spectrum, what we also find is that demand exceeds supply regularly, ironically because our education system has successfully ensured that almost every citizen reaches minimal education standards.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: Of course, apprenticeships themselves can also vary in appeal but that really brings us back to the key driver, in my view, behind the polarisation process, and that is the race for the best paying jobs.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: We should not underestimate the effort required to make apprenticeships attractive even under SkillsFuture.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: Expectations will build about SkillsFuture, about how it will aid in protecting our workforce against specific longer-term challenges caused by outdated and inadequate skills.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: Some types of expectation, however, will have to be tempered by reality.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: Employers will still have to contend with a tight supply of manpower in the short run, even as they participate in schemes to provide training places which are aimed at addressing their long-term needs.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: And there will be some 	Page: 57 tension between the two, which employers will look to the new agency to help them navigate.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: In any case, an important aspect of SkillsFuture is the emphasis on relevant skills.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: As the SkillsFuture initiative progresses and as the agency develops as an institution, just as with other institutions in Singapore, anticipation will also begin to grow about funding.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: Adequate funding is clearly important, and a lack of resources can severely impede progress of the initiative.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: However, I hope we will be cognitive of the fact that while national funding is necessary, it is only one of several factors that are needed to ensure that demands for the provision of adult education are met.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: By itself, funding is not sufficient and we should be mindful not to trigger a spiral in which funds chase after limited resources.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: Rather, the alignment of the agency's goals with the long-term aspirations of the Singapore workforce, as well as the commitment of individual workers to the fundamental ideal of a desire for self-improvement, is much more important.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: I would now like to point out two areas, which are related to each other, which I hope the Minister can provide some clarification on.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: My concern is not with the designation of productivity improvement as a clear goal, because this is part of the bold vision of the Bill that I clearly support.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: My concern is that if the difficulties with productivity measurement are not qualified, whether this would mire the agency before it even gets around to dealing with the core of the issue.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: While the primary concern at this point in time is how to make up our productivity shortfall, the SkillsFuture drive itself is much more important for the long term.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: SkillsFuture looks at capacity building, without which not just productivity but the essential viability of our local workforce will be called into question.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: One way to look at this difference is to ask how critical productivity actually is.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: Of course, without productivity, we all know that we would not be able to justify our wage increases.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: However, how critical then is the SkillsFuture drive?

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: The latter could lead to a litany of problems, such as a lack of competitiveness, unemployment and under-employment, all of which other economies are painfully familiar with.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: Next, there is also the difference between the long term and short term in considering the performance of the economy.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: In some cases, one may have to allow for a trade-off.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: For the present Bill, this should be particularly relevant because education and training often require making short-term sacrifices.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: This is something which students I meet in UniSIM, adult workers and adult learners are very familiar with.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: I think it is very important to emphasise the long term because this is where personal drive and motivation have a critical bearing on the final outcomes.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: When the going gets tough, individual motivation will be needed to make the final mile.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: This is particularly timely, in view of the current juncture which our economy has reached.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: Workers in possession of a strong foundation of relevant skills are needed in order to be able to maintain an even keel during the ongoing process of deep restructuring, as well as to embrace the future economy with confidence.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: In a dynamic and globally competitive environment, such workers will be able to provide the drive and steering needed for a vision of the future.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: (In Mandarin):   Mdm Speaker, as Acting Minister Ong Ye Kung once said in this House, "Our children are growing up in a new world, striking paths into a Singapore that is more inclusive, all-embracing, and a place where we can celebrate diverse talents and gifts.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Education must be at the heart of this journey, guiding them in purpose, equipping them with skills and helping them seize the opportunities of their age." I could not agree more with the vision Acting Minister Ong has set out.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: We need to support Singaporeans to find and pursue all kinds of dreams.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: This is vastly different from a traditional education system.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: So, SkillsFuture Singapore will have to change mindsets at the national level.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: This is a very important mandate that cannot be achieved overnight.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: For example, we all know that programming, learning to deal with machine learning and artificial Intelligence are all important.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: We also need to incorporate such future-oriented skillsets into our curriculum.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: I hope that SkillsFuture can provide insights into how our children can come into contact with various new areas.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: SkillsFuture needs to align itself with the maps and support Singaporeans to develop mastery that the market needs.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: So, I hope that our public can give the SkillsFuture agency more time to work hand in hand with our economic and manpower agencies so that we can get our plans right as much as possible.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: I hope that SkillsFuture and WSG can look into this.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: We all know that many mature and disabled workers feel very apprehensive about the future.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Despite that, some employers still do not want to risk hiring mature workers, especially when these workers do not have the relevant work experience.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Many mature and disabled workers I talk to do not even get the chance to get interviewed.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: I believe the sharing economy can be the light at the end of the tunnel for them because, for consumers, the risk they undertake when they parcel out a one-off job is far smaller.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: For example, if you are taking a ride from Uber or finding someone to do electrical work or plumbing on ServisHero, the consumer does not ask about the age or unrelated disabilities of the person providing the service.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: What matters is whether they get good reviews.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: At the same time, the sharing economy provides choices if our people do not want to or cannot work full time.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: They can make use of opportunities that the sharing economy affords.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: While such job opportunities in the sharing economy are largely service-related, over time, the opportunities created could be more diverse.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)

text: Page: 60 Of course, there are mature and disabled workers who still need full-time jobs.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: The young should learn skills and acquire knowledge in careers or jobs which they desire and must long to deepen their skills.

text: And those in employment or are retrenched should be given an opportunity to develop in new industries with suitable relevant skills.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: As what Peter Senge said, one must be willing to "learn, unlearn and relearn" and to add more, be willing to embrace lifelong learning as this is the part that we savour as Singapore's deoxyribonucleic acid (DNA) for the workforce of today and tomorrow and for years to come.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: An article by Minister Ong Ye Kung published on The Straits Times website on 21 April 2016 eloquently explains that "SkillsFuture is about three big ideas", more appropriately known as a movement instead of just a scheme, as it encompasses the three "M"s.

text: It involves continuous learning and being at the top of the game or craft.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: And the third "M" is "Meritocracy" which means recognising a person for being good at what he is doing.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: It needs all parties, not limited to the Government, but employers, associations, licensing bodies and unions, to commit to come together to ensure employability of our people so as to meet the needs of our economy.

text: Can the Minister consider an active involvement of the unions with the young but soon-to-be working people?

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Page: 62 Recently, I attended a presentation by a company on their masterplan to use new technology and automation going forward.

text: They showed a nice video where goods and vehicles are moving fast and autonomously.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: However, during the break, the worker came up to me.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: He could not find himself in the video.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: His job was not in the video, not in the future of the company.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Our future generations of workers must understand the importance of acquiring work-ready skills and they must never stop learning.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Likewise, our older workers need to embrace learning so that they continue to stay relevant.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Current skill sets need to be upgraded and new skills need to be acquired so that our workers remain employable and are able to add value to their jobs.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: In this speech, let me focus on the mid-career workers, in particular, PMEs, and how more can be done to ensure that the SkillsFuture initiative impacts them positively.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Many of our mid-career PMEs, having worked in a particular industry or in a certain job function for a number of years, become contented in their "comfort zones".

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: We need our PMEs to, first, find it within themselves to want to explore or learn new skills and develop their interests professionally.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Such is best exemplified by the "MasterChef" reality television series, where individuals participate in a slew of gruelling cooking contests to become professional chefs.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: These contestants come from all walks of life.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Regardless of age, they have something in common – that passion for cooking, and they are not afraid to pursue their dream of becoming a professional chef.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: SSG will need to explore ways and deepen its efforts in helping people understand and appreciate the value of the training courses available.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Communication channels must be targeted effectively towards the different groups, different segments of workers.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Thirdly, we need the strong support of employers.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: A nurturing company that is willing to invest in the continuous training and lifelong learning needs of its employees will see that their employees are more loyal and more motivated.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: When the trained staff applies newly acquired knowledge to their work, it helps to boost the productivity levels of the company.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: As SSG strives to establish a comprehensive learning infrastructure, I urge Singaporeans, especially our PMEs, to spare a portion of their valuable time and invest it in skills upgrading.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
