speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: (In Mandarin):   Mdm Speaker, having read the objectives and functions of the SSG, I support the SkillsFuture Singapore Agency Bill.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: This Bill brings vocational education and lifelong learning under the jurisdiction of MOE.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: This is a very fundamental change in the national education concept.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: In order for this concept to succeed, we cannot just rely on the Government and Statutory Boards.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: It is important for all enterprises and trade associations to be actively involved.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: Changes in Singapore's demography have already created serious manpower challenges.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: The ageing population, higher educational standards, low fertility rates and the continued decline in new workforce are some of the contributing factors.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: At the same time, some workers lack the skills to cope with the restructuring economy, and, with the curbs on foreign workers, the manpower woes faced by businesses are becoming more apparent.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: Even as businesses are unable to find workers, there are reports in the media on university graduates who are unable to find jobs.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: This predicament prompts the question of whether the nurturing of talent via our education system has been too advanced to match real market needs.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: Students are educated in an ideal environment, with the latest technology.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: However, when they enter the job market, they may find that the work requirements are less advanced than the skills they had learnt.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: Under the coordination of MOE, SSG could work closely with ITEs, polytechnics, universities and private training institutes to make timely adjustments to the skills training framework according to 	Page: 64 market requirements.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: However, my reservation is that once SSG comes under MOE, would MOE have a comprehensive understanding of employment needs?

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: At this stage of economic transformation, market changes are not only accelerated but complex.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: Emerging industries need manpower, and so do traditional industries, while MNCs have the greatest appeal for young people.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: When the Government started to promote SkillsFuture, large companies started to get involved and provided internship opportunities to compete for the best talent.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: In this regard, SMEs are at a real disadvantage.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: In the current vocational education system, including polytechnics and ITEs, there has always been a mismatch in supply and demand.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: Some students are choosing a discipline blindly with no understanding of the industry.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: They only find out after graduating that they do not like what they studied.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: Some have graduated but do not enter the job market and hope to pursue further studies; there are other students whose areas of study are too advanced and cannot be applied in local enterprises.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: Enterprises can only function if they have people.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: Without people, it is pointless to discuss anything.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: Basically, we have to fill our stomachs before considering growth.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: In this area, trade associations can play an important role.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: Every trade and industry association fully understands their manpower needs and could provide the latest industry development scenarios.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: Local trade associations must collaborate closely with MOE and SSG to tailor the skills framework for specific industries and to make the necessary preparations for the future growth of their industries.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: Grooming talent entails a continuous process and mutual coordination.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: Participating in the training process as early as possible could narrow the gap between manpower needs and the supply of talent.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: Hence, I earnestly hope that MOE could balance the relations between the education system and manpower needs, and that in this crucial period of economic restructuring, it could adapt to the changes in the environment and restructure the workforce to continually provide the Singapore economy with skilled and quality talent, and enable each and every Singaporean to realise his or her full potential.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: New developments in technology are driving change at our workplace at an unprecedented pace.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Without constant refreshment and upgrading, our workforce will find it increasingly difficult to stay relevant in the global market.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Page: 65 SkillsFuture allows Singaporeans to take ownership of their own learning and is flexible enough to support evolving career needs and personal interests at different life stages.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Individuals can choose from a wide range of studies and skillsets from various accredited institutions island-wide.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: My main concern, however, is how to get our seniors to benefit from SkillsFuture and develop the relevant skills.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: I acknowledge that our elderly are not a homogenous group but, indeed, most of them are not as well-educated nor Internet-savvy.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: It is important for the Government to find out in greater detail what occupations our older workers and seniors are in, where they aspire to go in the next stage of their careers or post-retirement and develop related courses and programmes suitable for them.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: The difference in scores is among the widest, compared to other countries, although OECD attributed it to the reason that the survey was conducted in English here, which many of the older generation in Singapore are not as proficient in.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: This is a phenomenon of concern and should be rectified as we are a highly connected economy and depend heavily on ICT in the workplace.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Our older workers are, hence, particularly vulnerable if they are unable to keep up with developments in IT usage skills.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: This has a great impact on their ability to stay integrated at work, and those without IT skills will suffer from depressed wages or, even worse, retrenchment.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: English is the main language of the Internet and I would like to ask the Ministry how it intends to overcome the challenges of teaching seniors, who are more comfortable in their mother tongues, computer usage skills.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Will the Ministry need to open more English proficiency classes to cater to older Singaporeans, especially those from the lower-income groups who had little education in their youth?

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: I was heartened to read a recent press report that our polytechnics had increases of between 15% and over 60% in part-time students over the last few years.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: More and more of those in their 50s or 60s are signing up for part-time diploma courses, attending classes after a long day at work.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: They shared with the journalist that they were usually tired but persevered because they wanted to improve themselves and got a sense of satisfaction from learning something new.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: I hope the Government will eventually look into mandatory time-off for upgrading courses to be hardwired into employment contracts to support employees' upgrading.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Singapore's working hours are amongst the longest in the world but we are not the most productive.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: This indicates that our work culture and employers' attitude need to change from emphasising "face time" to focusing on efficiency and actual work done.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Mandating a prerequisite number of hours to be set aside for upgrading courses will help to keep our workforce up to date and enable them to be more 	Page: 66 productive.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: We started in 1979 with SDF as our first training initiative at the national level.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Today, we are about to welcome a brand new agency to helm the national objective of continued learning.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: In this regard, I stand in full support of the Bill.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: A culture of constant upskilling must be instilled among Singaporeans to help them stay ahead of changing workplace trends.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: SkillsFuture will provide them with a window to explore alternative skills and career tracks with little opportunity cost as they can pursue classes alongside their full-time jobs.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Clause 5(1)(h) highlights accreditation of providers of adult education.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: How does the Government decide which private education courses enjoy accreditation and which do not?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: For example, if a Singaporean would like to pick up a course on film-making, there is currently only one SkillsFuture-approved institution and course available, although there are many similar courses available in the market.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: It is also the students themselves who can best testify if the courses are relevant to their needs.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I could not agree more with the importance of this function.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: This ensures that we do not miss the point that as we encourage adults to embark on self-improvement, we do not run the risk of turning adult learning into a mere paper chase.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: A certificate is not an end-all, and what this new agency must focus on is to instil a genuine curiosity for learning, a desire for self-improvement and the resolve to take ownership of one's career.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: These are the hallmarks of a motivated, robust and highly adaptable workforce, ready to take on the rapid changes in the 21st century workplace.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Employability is measured by a complex matrix of attributes, including not just hard skills, but inherent behavioural attributes, such as resilience, creativity, risk-taking and curiosity – traits which are not often considered the core strengths of the Singaporean workforce.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: These are soft skills which can never be taught in a classroom, much like attempting to teach children moral values 	Page: 67 through textbooks.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: As we shine the spotlight on adult learning, I urge that we continue our efforts to improve the mainstream education system, giving children space outside of the classroom to acquire soft skills and instilling a genuine desire for self-learning and discovery from a young age.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: These comments notwithstanding, Madam, this Bill can only serve the interests of Singapore's workforce, and I stand in support of it.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I strongly support the establishment and the functions and powers of SSG.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: There are, however, a few suggestions that I have which I hope MOE will consider in finalising the functions and powers of SSG.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: And I trust that SSG will continue the work of CPE in monitoring the quality of programmes and courses provided by these PEIs.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: We must recognise that when our people go for further training or upgrading courses with such post-secondary institutions and other providers of adult or further education, the expectation is that the new qualification or certification of skills that they obtain, can help them progress in their careers or have better job prospects.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Hence, it is equally important for SSG to work closely with these institutions and providers to ensure that the programmes or courses provided are relevant to the requirements of the global and local markets.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: It is a shame if even after undergoing further training, skills training or upgrading programmes, one is not able to have better job prospects or progress in one's career.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: In addition, there are also smaller private companies or organisations that conduct non-academic programmes, such as culinary or coaching courses, which are also useful in helping us upgrade and further hone our skills that may be useful for career progression or even to take up a distinctly different second career.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I hope that SSG will also consider working with such companies or organisations, provided that they are able to prove their track records and the content and credibility of their training courses.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I believe that one of the 	Page: 68 objectives of SSG is to train and help our people be future- and global-ready.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Hence, it is imperative that the members and advisors of SSG be those with relevant and adequate global experience and skills which are dynamic and current.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: (In Malay):   SkillsFuture will provide a wider platform for our community to continue upgrading their skills and obtain certifications that will provide various job opportunities.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I hope that our community will seize the opportunities that are available through the initiatives and programmes under SkillsFuture.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: SkillsFuture can help those who wish to change their careers receive training and obtain skills that will be relevant to their new careers.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I would also like to urge our community to understand that the opportunities presented through SkillsFuture are not limited to enhancing the knowledge and skills that are relevant to their careers.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: SkillsFuture also provides opportunities for us to pursue lifelong learning so that we can continue to be active even as we get older.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I believe that SkillsFuture will be useful in the active ageing process of our community.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: (In English): Mdm Speaker, notwithstanding those few areas of concern that I have expressed earlier, I fully support the SkillsFuture Singapore Agency Bill.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: May the establishment of SSG provide more and better opportunities for our people in terms of education, training, retraining and skills upgrading and, thereafter, better employability and employment prospects.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: This shows the Government's commitment to helping Singaporean workers survive and thrive in a world that is changing faster than ever.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Meanwhile, real wages in the US have been basically stagnant over the past four decades, and in Britain and Germany, they have been stagnant over the past decade.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: I think we can see how that has affected their societies and politics.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: By contrast, Singapore has managed to protect rank-and-file workers, to a certain extent, against global trends of technology displacing workers.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Wage increased 1.1%, but productivity only increased 0.4%.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: So, we have some way to go in our productivity drive.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Given that sectors with higher productivity growth have higher real wage growth, productivity growth is key to our workers doing well in the years to come.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: I have noticed an issue in our push towards continuous learning and high productivity.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: From the feedback from my residents, it seems like there may be some mismatch.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: The courses that the residents wanted to take are not in the list of SkillsFuture Credit courses.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: And these are qualifications that are highly sought after in the marketplace.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Perhaps, there are other professional courses that the residents wanted to take as well.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: I think SSG will have to periodically review the courses offered and include courses that Singaporeans request for if they are suitable.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: This will enable it to fulfil its mission of funding courses that are responsive to the needs of industry.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Another potential issue is the number of people using their SkillsFuture credits.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: But the number could taper off as many people do not find the time or motivation to upgrade themselves.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: I hope SSG will come up with a plan to reach out to Singaporeans who have not used their credits yet.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: SSG could remind them of their credits and offer guidance on how to use them.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: There are also course providers who jumped onto the bandwagon, hoping to make money from the Government.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: According to my residents, there are course providers who hard-sell their courses at shopping centres and busy town centres.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: According to one resident, he was approached by a course provider at Khatib central.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: So, he was told, "You don't need to pay.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: At the end of the course, you will get a free iPad." He signed up for an English course for adults.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: And he said that when he started to attend the class, the course instructor was not well-prepared and was from another country which is predominantly Chinese-speaking.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: The way he puts it, "I hope there will be more audits on the quality of the instructors and how well prepared they are." Please allow me to summarise in Chinese.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: (In Mandarin):   The Government is setting up SSG to demonstrate our commitment to lifelong learning.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Data shows that after inflation adjustment, real wage in Singapore has grown 1.1% per year, higher than many developed countries.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: However, our productivity growth was only 0.4% per year.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Hence, we must raise our productivity so that Singaporeans' salaries can rise in tandem.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Some residents told me that the SkillsFuture credits cannot be used for some professional certifications, such as internal auditors or IT auditors.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: I hope SSG can periodically review people's feedback, and consider adding or removing some courses.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: After SSG is moved to MOE, I hope it will continue to communicate with MOM on our manpower needs and promote lifelong learning to benefit Singaporeans.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: (In English): We can continue to coordinate manpower needs so as to maximise its benefits to our economy and our people.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: This is a very exciting mission ahead and a new structure for us "to chase our own rainbows".

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: We are saying you need to build a foundation of skills, of depth, and with that, we can build our future.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: If you are in a traditional industry, you must have that and then you can compete globally and regionally.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: If you are in a new area, you also need that.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: I was walking out of the Chamber and I bumped into him and his family.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: So, I asked him, "Tokyo 2020, are you going to compete in more events?" He said he would compete in the 100-metre freestyle, 200-metre butterfly, maybe individual medley.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: But I said, "Then why not this round?" He said he wanted to focus on 100-metre butterfly this round.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: When you focus on one area and you are excellent at it, it gives you the foundation to do many other things.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Versatility comes from depth, and I think we need to let all our workers know that we must really be excellent in our craft, and then we will have the versatility to move to new sectors.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: If we just touch the surface of everything, we will not have the versatility.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Mr Thomas Chua said he noticed that there is a slight drop in the employment outcomes of our graduates and a slight increase in the unemployed graduates.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: He said he is a little bit worried "他有一点点担心".

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Not for now, because I think slight changes in employment outcomes for our undergraduates, for our graduates coming out from universities will happen as the economy goes up and down.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: But what I am very worried about whether is 10 or 20 years from now, we will continue to be able to achieve this kind of excellent employment outcomes for our graduates, both from the ITEs, polytechnics, as well as from our universities?

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Today, the part in MOE dealing with higher education, there is a very acute awareness of the need for industry, that we have to produce graduates that are needed by the industries.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: How else will we achieve high employment outcomes if we do not have that mindset?

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: What I am very worried about is how do we sustain that for the long term, say, 10 years, 20 years down the road?

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Mr Desmond Choo expressed a similar concern whether by moving SSG to MOE, will we dilute the focus on industry and only focus on the young.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: This has also been our preoccupation for the longest time.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Today, all the curricula of all our programmes are done in consultation with the industry.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: I think the best way is we take an outfit which has deep knowledge in engaging industries, which understands the philosophy of adult training very well and inject them into MOE.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: This is why we restructured WDA and placed SSG within MOE, so that we can work with the industry and understand the philosophy of adult training even better.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: To do this, I think there are two caveats.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: First, this should not dilute the research efforts of our universities.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: In fact, I think there is concern on the other side of the House which does research on 	Page: 71 whether this industry focus will dilute research efforts.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Second, if there are company-specific skills, sometimes, it is better to be taught in the company because, if it is so specific, I think the company should take it up.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: There was a suggestion by Mr Henry Kwek that coding is now very "in", needed by many industries, and whether we should start to put them into our curriculum.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Likewise, you can make a similar argument for data science, and I think all our IHLs – polytechnics and universities are today, starting these courses, whether it is coding or data science.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: But I will just be cautious – my colleague Minister Ng Chee Meng, who is not here, has also been very cautious – to put this content into the primary school curricula.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: We all know our school kids are already quite stressed with a very heavy curriculum.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Sometimes, when it is so industry-specific, you might want to leave it to later when you are in an IHL.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: For younger students, give them the important foundational skills, usually literacy, numeracy and values.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: There was a large point made by Ms Denise Phua which is that, for SSG to do well, we have to do better in terms of content, pedagogy or andragogy, as well as assessment.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: How to learn, when to learn, what to learn and how to assess?

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: All these are part of the philosophy of adult workers' training, which is very different from teaching and educating a student.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: And SSG has done a lot of work in this.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: It even has a research outfit to research into adult training philosophy.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: All that, we will now inject into MOE to uplift our capabilities in this area.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: But to do well, we have to make collaborations and partnerships with many partners, as many Members have pointed out.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: This is a point made by Mr Thomas Chua, Mr Melvin Yong and also Ms Thanaletchimi.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: There are many existing efforts already in place.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: For example, we have the Sectoral Tripartite Committees (STC).

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: This is formed at each sector, and within each committee, we always have industry and company representatives to guide the work of the STCs.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: We also work with associations and chambers, including for training delivery.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: The latest was the logistics industry which is now also delivering training for the industry.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: It is definitely a priority we will look at.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: We are also working on cooperative education programmes, which we announced some time ago.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Cooperative programmes mean there is cooperation between the universities and industries.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: It is different from just an internship where you study three years and, for three to six months, you are out in the company doing work, sometimes ending up photocopying a lot, or buying coffee.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: But a cooperative programme is much more than that.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: You spend a whole semester on campus studying the theory and then another entire semester working in a company, working on actual projects.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: The big difference is that the company and the universities are working together to design the curriculum.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: You are bringing the industry into the universities.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Page: 72 It is a point also made by Mr Louis Ng that this is actually the best way to learn soft skills.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: I always find people describe soft skills and technical skills as a T-shaped skill.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: It is actually quite an unfortunate description because first, you assume that they are distinct and separate.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Second, because of the way you write "T", it implies that learning soft skills and technical skills are sequential.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: It is more like an "A", you start with nothing, and then you go deep and broad at the same time.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: We learn generic skills in the context of practising our technical skills.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: With a cooperative programme, students get to work on actual projects, which is when they practise their technical skills and, at the same time, learn the generic skills – teamwork, management, HR, getting along with people, working across cultures.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: You have to put them in the context of a real technical project.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: This will be our form of apprenticeships, whether it is ELP or cooperative programmes.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: We will expand them, and extend it to not just the young but also the not so young.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: For companies, too, they will have a big role to play, in the way they choose to hire, reward and promote.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: If what all companies do is look at academic results and hire and promote based on academic results, it would miss the point of SkillsFuture.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Companies have to look deep to understand what kind of competencies they are looking for, who are displaying those competencies, who are performing well at the job?

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: If enough companies do that and it becomes the mainstream way of developing our human resource, then the signal to Singaporean workers and students is very clear.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: It is your competency and skills that matter, not just your grades.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Grades matter a lot, but as you step into the workforce, it is your competency, how well you are performing at the job that matters.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: I strongly urge companies to go out, tweak your HR systems, emphasise competency.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: As you do so, mature workers will have greater chances to get employed.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Today, many mature workers do not get a chance even to be interviewed because maybe years ago when they were 18 or 21, their academic results were not as strong.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: But they might have made up for that with years of experience and doing well in their jobs.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: They should be recognised as they apply for new jobs or seek new careers.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Besides companies, unions will play a critical role.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: It is a specific point raised by Ms Thanaletchimi.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: For unions, the role is especially important in guiding workers because you have 60 to 62 unions now, with wide outreach channels to workers.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: You also have institutions like the e2i that also has separate outreach platforms to workers.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Mr Thomas Chua, Mr Melvin Yong, Ms Joan Pereira, all pointed out the importance of helping to communicate and guide workers on how to use their $500 credit.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Once this restructuring is done, we will have a team in MOE, within ITE, the universities and polytechnics who will help to guide students.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: We also have a team in WDA today doing the same thing for workers but, at the same time, they are in partnership with e2i, the unions, self-help groups and also trade associations and chambers.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: They are all what you would describe as independent coaches, which is what Ms Thanaletchimi described.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: With the restructuring, we can bring them all together, coordinate their efforts, reach out to Singaporean workers and guide them in the use of their SkillsFuture credits in a much more coordinated and effective way.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Page: 73 And this is something, a priority, that we want to look into.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Several Members have raised concerns about specific groups.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: And I do agree with the Member that we can do a lot more in language training.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Language training, whether it is English, Chinese, Malay, Tamil, is also a lifelong pursuit.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: We have to get better and better at the language, through lifelong learning.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: The fortunate thing is that WDA, over many years, has developed the Workplace Literacy and Numeracy training framework which supports language training.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: It is not academic in nature but tailored to meet the needs of the workforce.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: They have done that and they have trained tens of thousands of workers.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: I think we should see how we can proliferate that so that more seniors can benefit from language training.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: The next group that needs special attention are persons with disabilities.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: That is the point that Ms Denise Phua had raised.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: We will do several things to help persons with disabilities even more.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: In a way, that could be the nucleus of what the Member described as a special education academy over time.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Second, I still remember the Member and Ms Chia Yong Yong, who is not here, had requested, during the Committee of Supply debate, that MOE review the Post-Secondary Education Account (PSEA) to see whether we can relax the rules so that persons with disabilities can use the money more flexibly.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: This is a first-stop office for students who require special education assistance.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: It will coordinate all the support, including counselling and workshops, for the students who have special education needs.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: It also administers the Special Education Needs (SEN) Fund.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: The students can tap on this fund to buy devices, such as hearing and visual aids that can help them with their education journey.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: At the same time, they will also train academic staff so that they have basic special needs awareness.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: So, these are all the things we are doing.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: I am of the view that there is space for a place like a special education academy or SG Enable that is focused on helping the disabled.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: There is also a space for everyone else to do their bit.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: At Bizlink, they do not profess to take in people with all disabilities.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: They have three or four kinds of work which were suitable for persons with certain disabilities, and they try to fit each individual to the work.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Likewise, I think every company and institution must look at disabilities by asking themselves which individuals they can help and then go out to help them.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: It is not possible for a single agency or institution to cater to disabilities of all forms.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: A third group, raised by Mr Leon Perera, is ex-offenders.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: WDA, even before SSG, has been working with the Singapore Corporation of Rehabilitative Enterprises (SCORE) for quite some time.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: It is part of the Yellow Ribbon project.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: They have a project called Project Phoenix through which they help inmates to re-integrate by going into industries, such as culinary, retail and other services.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: This is ongoing and is certainly an area that we can do more over time.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: But as SCORE always says, imprisonment is one issue, but when you are released, society can imprison you 	Page: 74 again.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: So, again, industry, companies, agencies, we can all do our bit, each one of us.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: If we are a bit more open-hearted, I think ex-offenders will be able to integrate into society much more.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: The other important stakeholder is the training industry.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Dr Intan Mokhtar pointed out the need for us to work with the private education industry as well.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: We always have different tiers in our partnerships with private training providers.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: The first tier is what we called the Continuing Education and Training (CET) Centres.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: They could offer courses in film-making, digital animation or culinary arts.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: We work closely with them to build up the curriculum, accredit their programmes in line with industry needs, set out their objectives clearly, make sure that the courses are open to all.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: We buy training places from them, audit the quality of the programmes very tightly and also measure the outcomes.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: So, in response to Mr Leon Perera, we do have such a system to support individuals in skills development for more expensive courses.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: We actually put in a lot more resources to buy the training places so that a member of the public can attend those pre-subsidised programmes, except that we do this on the supply end, whereas SkillsFuture Credit is funding at the demand end.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: We fund at the supply end because we have to be assured that the supply is of good quality.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Beyond the 40-over CET Centres today, WDA also supports a lot of training in other areas, including in-company training.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Some areas of training are useful and we should look at those.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: This would include, maybe, internal audit or IT audit that Er Dr Lee Bee Wah mentioned.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: If there are, indeed, programmes that help our workers professionally, to deepen their skills or chart a new career, we should look at them.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: There are plenty of precedents for us to do so.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: There are many of them because we started off with an inclusive approach and because there were so many workers that needed training.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: So, whenever we get a suggestion to include a particular course, we do some audit and checks.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: If the course meets our criteria, we include it in the course directory.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: That is why, over the last few months, we built it up to 15,000 courses.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: In fact, the complaint we usually hear is with so many courses, how to choose?

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Which goes back to the issue of guidance.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: But over time, we will have to start streamlining the list of courses and step up audits on training providers.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: This is a point also raised by Mr Louis Ng which I think is very valid.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: We have some upfront checks and some regular audits.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Over time, we need to make use of the power of public feedback.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Trainees who attend the courses can rate them and there will be user reviews.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: So, if you attend a language course where your English is better than the trainer, you can put in the feedback and your rating.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: No different from shopping on Amazon or Taobao.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: This is a feature that we will put into the ILP.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: There is a comment, by Dr Intan Mokhtar and Ms Thanaletchimi, on PEIs which deliver degree programmes to young people.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: The latter attend those courses, get their degrees and then are disappointed because they did not get the jobs they wished to have.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: We totally understand that for the young, they want to get a degree.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: We should support as many of our young people to get degrees, provided that our economy can sustain that many graduates.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: At the same time, we have to make sure that the degree they get is 	Page: 75 something that the industry needs.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: If not, it will be very frustrating for our young graduates.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: So, as I have mentioned in this House before, we need to have more transparency about the employment outcomes for graduates of PEIs.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: I think this is a point that Mr Leon Perera made as well.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: We should do more so that students have the information to decide whether to take up the courses.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Where possible, try to shift them from providing just general degrees that maybe the industry does not need, to SkillsFuture-related programmes that the industry needs.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: We will do the students a big service by doing so.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: The SSG board, and this is a point raised by Dr Intan Mokhtar and Ms Thanaletchimi, must have a good mix of members representative of our partners and stakeholders.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: I will maintain the character of the current WDA board which largely comprises industry representatives, with a sprinkling of different expertise from other sectors, including from the unions, and people who are well-versed in finance and audit.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: As I mentioned very early on, we are not diluting or trying to change the character of WDA.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: We are taking their DNA and injecting into MOE.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: But it will not be possible for every sector to be represented.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: The Bill only provides for 15 people on the board.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: We will supplement that with the Sectoral Tripartite Committees that we have.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: As the saying goes, if you do not measure, it does not matter.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: For us to want to do something well, there has to be some measurement.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: This is also an issue about vision and plan.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Vision with no plan is just a dream; a plan with no vision, you are just busy for nothing.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: So, there must be both a vision for the long term and a plan for the short and medium term.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: For the short term, there has to be a plan that is aligned with what we want to achieve.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: These will be plans that are within SSG's control.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: These are pretty much measuring what kind of output they will deliver in the short term.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: For example, how many ELPs you will roll out, what is the training participation rate, how many students or workers you will give guidance to, to bring them into the training and development journey, how many SkillsFuture Study Awards and SkillsFuture Fellowships you will be issuing and awarding, how many cooperative programmes we will roll out.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: But it is harder to measure progress in the medium to long term.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: In reply to Mr Leon Perera's point, academics and other individuals who have been studying this area have done so for many years, and it is still very difficult to draw causality between training and employment outcomes.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: You can draw correlation, but it is very difficult to draw causality because there are so many factors at play.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: There is the Kirkpatrick Model, which I assume the Member is familiar with.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Every year, WDA does a survey to collect feedback on employment outcomes from training and the results are published every year.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: In that survey, they measure whether, first, the trainee is satisfied with the training; second, after he starts work, is the employer satisfied with the training; third, is there an assessment that he is performing better after the training; fourth, did he get promoted or get a pay 	Page: 76 rise after the training.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: I think every few years, we ought to do something; if anything, just to satisfy ourselves that the correlation is still there even if we cannot prove causality.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: In the very long term, ultimately, we want to raise productivity; we want to raise competitiveness for the Singapore economy.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: I think we cannot rely on one measure because every sector measures productivity and competitiveness differently.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: It also should not just be SSG's KPI; these are the collective KPIs of all the agencies which are involved.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: That is why we have so many agencies involved in each Sectorial Tripartite Committee.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Other than economic competitiveness and productivity, SkillsFuture goes beyond being just an economic movement in the longer term.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Ultimately, we want Singaporean workers to want to master something, just like how Joseph Schooling mastered swimming.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: We all define ourselves often, not just by who we are, where we are born, but also what we are good at, what is our profession.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: That mastery is as important to a person's identity.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: With mastery, we can do something very well and that is when we can derive our future competitiveness.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: If we encourage these multiple pathways for every Singaporean to chase their own rainbows and be good at what they are doing in their respective fields, we will have a much more inclusive, much broader concept of meritocracy.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: We embrace them all and society recognises them all.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Restructuring of SSG is just one small step, it is the starting point.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: We are really combining the tremendous delivery capability of MOE with the adult learning philosophy of WDA into one Ministry.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: This is not just an SSG endeavour but it is a Singapore endeavour for the long term.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: I would just like to thank the Minister for the explanations.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: He engaged very deeply on all the points that were made, so I thank him for that.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: My point on pushing education to prisoners was actually referring to prisoners who are currently serving their sentence.

speaker: Mdm Speaker
text: I suspend the Sitting and will take the Chair again at 4.15 pm.

speaker: Mdm Speaker
